This sound burst sailors' eardrums 64 kilometers away.
In 1883, the Krakatoa volcano in Indonesia blew itself apart, and over 36,000 people died.
4,800 kilometers away, on Rodrigues Island, police heard it and thought it was distant cannon fire.
160 kilometers away, a gas gauge recorded a blast equal to 172 decibels. Louder than a jet engine up close.
Then the pressure wave kept going. Barometers around the world caught it circling the Earth at least 3 times.
Two thirds of the island vanished, and ash turned sunsets blood red across the world for months.
In 1927, a new volcano rose in the same spot. Its name means Child of Krakatoa. And it's still erupting.
